messages.subject: compare data from two sites
messages.body_plain:
Hello dear all, I am new at the hirarchical model, so perhaps my questions are very simple. If this is not the correct place to ask them, I would be grateful of receiving some advice of a better place to ask. I am working with a data set of two different ranches and I am running an HDS model. My intention is to copare densities in both sites so I am running the model using one data set which contains information of both sites and then I intend to separate them by including the site name as a covariable. Is this correct?
Thank you very much in  advance.
Regards
Antonela

messages.subject: Re: compare data from two sites
messages.body_plain:
Hi there!

When you say HDS, you mean Hierarchical Distance Sampling? I'm also quite new here (and to hierarchical modeling) but figured I'd post; My interpretation is that your method would be correct - just run a null model (accounting for imperfect detection, of course) and another that is the same but includes a covariate for "site". Using this, you can get "Site"-specific estimates of density.

Which analysis software do you intend to use?

Good luck!!
DJ

messages.subject: Distance-based Analysis For Transect Data -- Ideas?
messages.subject_clean: Distance-based Analysis For Transect Data -- Ideas?
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone!

DJ McNeil (2nd year PhD Student) here! So I'm working on a new (to me) problem that I suspect some of you have encountered in the past... I have transects (~1km in length) within different habitats. Each transect has associated habitat data - categorical (like forest type) and continuous (like % canopy cover). We surveyed along each transect for birds and, and, each time we detected the bird along the transect, we recorded the perpendicular distance from the transect (see fig below). I would like to conduct some sort of distance-based analysis in a hierarchical framework, however, I'm not sure where I should begin. My goals are to 1) account to imperfect detection 2) evaluate baseline bird density and 3) evaluate the effects of habitat covariates on density (conifer forest vs deciduous... % canopy on density, etc.). I've done two types of distance-based analyses in the past (only with point transects - never line transects); the offset-based model by Solymos et al. (2013, cited below) as well as within program DISTANCE.

With this in mind, I'm not sure that the Solymos method is best suited to transect data and, being totally honest, it was a bit clunky to use (though I'm willing to do it if makes sense). I should also say that Dr. Solymos has been HUGELY helpful when I was doing those previous analyses ... But I digress - I'm wondering what's the best way to go? If I'm not mistaken, program DISTANCE does not allow the inclusion of covariates which affect density (only those which affect detection probability). I might consider something in the N-mixture framework but I would think that repeat surveys would be needed. I'm FAIRLY new to this type of work but I'm reasonably familiar some common point count analysis techniques - single season occupancy models and N-mixture models. I'm not looking to do anything super crazy but would love to learn something new, particularly if it's a flexible tool :-)

Thanks in advance, everyone!

DJ

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-Pgs0oNFAgbk/WCtyOLn26JI/AAAAAAAABIU/cQxgY1JrKuwVX3yum83vz4RGz2GHhJkQwCLcB/s1600/TransectExample_McNeil.png>

Solymos, Peter, Steven M. Matsuoka, Erin M. Bayne, Subhash R. Lele, Patricia Fontaine, Steve G. Cumming, Diana Stralberg, Fiona KA Schmiegelow, and Samantha J. Song. "Calibrating indices of avian density from non‐standardized survey data: making the most of a messy situation." Methods in Ecology and Evolution 4, no. 11 (2013): 1047-1058.

messages.body_plain:
unmarked explicitly supports transect-based distance analysis that allows density to vary; it also happens to be very well supported (vignettes, a google group with a lengthy archive of questions/responses, the 2016 Kery and Royle AHM book, etc.) and is well-connected to many other R packages (raster, AICcModAv, and so forth).  And if you can't do what you need to do in unmarked, JAGS/BUGS typically can.  Not familiar with dsm, but it also seems pretty useful after taking a quick glance.

Royle et al. 2004 in Ecology might be a useful reference to start with.

messages.body_plain:
DJ,

Sorry for coming late to this discussion, you might have sorted out your approach already. Just wanted to confirm that the distance sampling approach implemented in detect::cmulti assumes circular point count geometry (triangular weight distribution) and not line transect (uniform).

This vignette walks you through the unmarked::distsamp function usage including line transects: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/unmarked/vignettes/distsamp.pdf

Note that detect::cmulti is conditional likelihood estimation, while unmarked::distsamp uses integrated likelihood for multinomial N-mixture.

Cheers,

Peter

ps: thanks for the nice words :)
